chapters.name: Boot Sector
chapters.line: Toolchain, modules and the test loop every level uses.

levels.title: Power On
levels.brief: Create the burrow module and a burrowd binary with a testable run() function, proper exit codes and usage text.
build: `go mod init burrow` (already done in this repo)
`cmd/burrowd/main.go` with `run(args, stdout, stderr) int`
`version`, `help` and usage errors with the right exit codes
levels.win: `burrowd version` prints `burrowd 0.1.0` and exits 0; usage mistakes exit 2 with usage on stderr; the built binary behaves the same.
hints: Keep `main` to one line: `os.Exit(run(os.Args[1:], os.Stdout, os.Stderr))`. Everything else lives in `run`, which tests can call.
A `switch args[0]` handles commands and their flag spellings together: `case "version", "-version", "--version":`.
Write usage once as a `const` string and print it with `fmt.Fprint(w, usage)` to whichever writer the case calls for.

levels.title: Test Bench
levels.brief: Learn the testing loop you'll use in every level after this one.
build: `store.ValidateKey(key string) error`
`var ErrInvalidKey`, wrapped with context using `%w`
Your own table-driven test in `store/validate_test.go`
levels.win: 25 valid/invalid keys classified correctly, errors wrap ErrInvalidKey, quote the key with %q, and stay short for huge keys.
hints: `len(s)` counts bytes, which is what the limit is in. `utf8.ValidString` checks encoding.
`for _, r := range key` walks runes, not bytes. Check `unicode.IsSpace(r) || unicode.IsControl(r)`.
For long keys, quote only a prefix: `fmt.Errorf("%w: %q... is %d bytes", ErrInvalidKey, key[:20], len(key))`.

chapters.name: Memory
chapters.line: An in-memory store that stays correct under concurrency.

levels.title: Register File
levels.brief: An in-memory key-value store with Get, Set, Delete and Len that gets missing keys, empty values and shared memory right.
build: `NewMemory()`, `Get`, `Set`, `Delete` (all take `ctx` first), `Len()`
`var ErrNotFound`
Copy byte slices on the way in and out
levels.win: Missing keys return ErrNotFound, empty values exist, no aliasing either way, cancelled contexts change nothing.
hints: Writing to a nil map panics. Make the map in `NewMemory`.
Slices share backing arrays. `bytes.Clone(v)` or `append([]byte(nil), v...)` makes an independent copy. Careful: `bytes.Clone(nil)` is nil, which is fine for storage but think about what Get returns.
Check `ctx.Err()` and `ValidateKey` at the top of each method, before touching the map.

levels.title: Bus Interface
levels.brief: Define the contract every storage engine in Burrow will satisfy.
build: `type Store interface` with Get, Set, Delete, Keys
`Memory.Keys(ctx, prefix)`, sorted
Pass the provided `storetest.Run` suite
levels.win: Memory satisfies store.Store and passes the full conformance suite.
hints: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly. Put the interface where it's used (here, package store) and keep it small.
`strings.HasPrefix` plus `slices.Sort` is all Keys needs. Sorting happens after you've collected matches.
A returned slice is a snapshot if you built it fresh. Don't return anything that points into your map.

levels.title: Arbiter
levels.brief: Make the store safe for many goroutines at once.
build: A `sync.RWMutex` in Memory
`Update(ctx, key, fn)`: atomic read-modify-write
Pass `storetest.RunConcurrent` under `-race`
levels.win: Race-free under the hammer, and 10,000 concurrent increments through Update land exactly.
hints: Lock inside methods, not in callers. A zero-value `sync.RWMutex` is ready to use; never copy a struct containing one.
Update holds the write lock for the whole read-call-write. That's what makes it atomic, and why fn must never call back into the store.
Give fn `append([]byte(nil), old...)` and store `append([]byte(nil), result...)`. Copies on both sides.

levels.title: Decay Timer
levels.brief: Keys that expire, and a background janitor you can stop cleanly.
build: Functional options: `WithClock`, `WithSweepInterval`, `WithOnEvict`
`SetWithTTL`, `TTL`, and expiry everywhere
A janitor goroutine and `Close()` that stops it
levels.win: Exact expiry on a fake clock, exactly-once eviction even with racing readers, OnEvict can re-enter the store, and Close leaves no goroutines.
hints: Store `expireAt time.Time` per entry (zero = never). Expired means `!now.Before(expireAt)`.
Exactly-once eviction: whoever deletes the entry under the write lock fires OnEvict. Re-check expiry after taking the lock; someone may have beaten you.
Collect evicted keys while locked, unlock, then call OnEvict. Close: `close(stop)` once via `sync.Once`, then wait on a `done` channel the janitor closes.

chapters.name: Wire
chapters.line: Raw TCP, your own protocol, a client and clean shutdown.

levels.title: Loopback
levels.brief: Your first network server: accept TCP connections and echo the bytes back.
build: `wire.ServeEcho(ln, logger) error`
One goroutine per connection, `io.Copy(conn, conn)`
slog lines with `remote` and `bytes` attributes
levels.win: Echoes 50 concurrent clients and 4 MiB payloads, handles half-close, returns nil when the listener closes.
hints: Accept blocks. `go handle(conn)` or the second client waits forever.
After `ln.Close()`, Accept returns an error matching `errors.Is(err, net.ErrClosed)`. That's your clean exit.
`io.Copy` returns the byte count you need for the `bytes` attribute. `slog.New(slog.DiscardHandler)` stands in for a nil logger.

levels.title: Line Protocol
levels.brief: A text protocol so you can drive the store by hand.
build: `wire.ServeLines(ln, st, logger) error`
SET/GET/DEL/KEYS/PING/QUIT with exact replies
Error replies, blank lines ignored, 64 KiB line limit
levels.win: Every command and error reply matches, pipelining and split writes work, long lines get `ERR line too long`.
hints: `strings.Cut(line, " ")` splits the command from the rest; cut the rest again for SET's key and value, so the value keeps its spaces.
`bufio.Scanner`'s default max token is 64 KiB. When it stops, check `errors.Is(sc.Err(), bufio.ErrTooLong)`.
Wrap the conn in a `bufio.Writer` and `Flush` after each command's reply, not after each line of KEYS.

levels.title: Framing
levels.brief: Text breaks on binary values. Replace it with length-prefixed frames.
build: `Op` constants and `Op.String()`
`WriteFrame` / `ReadFrame` with the exact byte layout
Size limits checked before allocating
levels.win: Golden bytes match, round trips survive slow readers, EOF rules are exact, oversized lengths don't allocate, and the fuzzer finds nothing.
hints: `conn.Read` can return fewer bytes than asked. `io.ReadFull` loops for you, and turns a mid-read EOF into `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF`.
Read the op byte separately: EOF there is a clean `io.EOF`; EOF anywhere after is unexpected.
Build the frame in one slice with `binary.BigEndian.AppendUint32` and write it once; compare `n` to `len(buf)` for `io.ErrShortWrite`.

levels.title: Client
levels.brief: A Go client package and a CLI, so you stop hand-typing frames.
build: `wire.Server` serving frames from a Store
`client` package: Dial, Get/Set/Delete/Ping, ServerError, ErrClosed
`cmd/burrowctl` with `-addr` and `-timeout`
levels.win: Deadlines and cancels return the context's error promptly, a timed-out connection is never reused, and 50 goroutines can share one client.
hints: Set the conn deadline from `ctx.Deadline()`, and use `context.AfterFunc(ctx, func(){ conn.SetDeadline(time.Unix(1,0)) })` so a cancel interrupts a blocked read.
When a call fails, check `ctx.Err()` first. The conn deadline can fire a hair before the context's timer, so also check whether the deadline has passed.
Any error mid-call leaves the stream out of sync: close the conn, set it to nil, and dial again on the next call. A mutex around each call keeps replies paired with requests.

levels.title: Power Down
levels.brief: Stop the server on Ctrl-C without dropping requests in flight.
build: `Server.Shutdown(ctx)` and `ErrServerClosed`
Track connections as idle or busy
`burrowd serve` with signal handling
levels.win: Idle connections close at once, in-flight requests finish, the context deadline force-closes, and the binary exits 0 on SIGINT and SIGTERM.
hints: Keep a set of connections and a busy flag on each, guarded by a mutex. Busy from a full request read until its reply is written.
Shutdown loop: close listeners, then every few ms close idle conns, until a WaitGroup of handlers is done or ctx ends.
`signal.NotifyContext(ctx, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)` gives you a context that's cancelled on Ctrl-C.

chapters.name: Persistence
chapters.line: A write-ahead log that survives kill -9. Needed before Consensus and the Service Bus branch, so take it whenever you like.

levels.title: Write-Ahead Log
levels.brief: Survive a restart by logging every write before applying it.
build: `wal.Open`, `Append`, `Replay`, `Close`
`durable.Open(dir)`: Memory + log, replayed on open
Only acknowledge after the record is synced
levels.win: Durable passes both conformance suites and every acknowledged write survives kill -9.
hints: Open with `os.O_RDWR|os.O_CREATE` and track your append offset, or use `O_APPEND`. Replay can read with `ReadAt` so it doesn't move the write position.
Validate and check existence before appending, so rejected writes never reach the log.
Encode each change as a `wire.Frame` (OpSet/OpDelete) inside the record. You already have a tested codec.

levels.title: Parity Bits
levels.brief: Detect torn and corrupt records instead of trusting the bytes on disk.
build: A CRC32 on every record, covering its length
Torn tails truncated on Open
Mid-log corruption reported as ErrCorrupt
levels.win: Every truncation and bit flip is handled: torn tails repaired, real corruption refused, no phantom records from zeros.
hints: Checksum the length bytes and the payload together. Then an all-zero header fails the check.
A bad record is a torn tail if it reaches the end of the file, or everything after it is zeros. Otherwise it's corruption.
Check the length against `MaxRecordSize` and the remaining file size before allocating.

levels.title: Compaction
levels.brief: Stop the log growing forever with snapshots and atomic file swaps.
build: `Store.Snapshot()`
Write tmp, fsync, rename, then reset the log
Load snapshot then replay log on Open
levels.win: The log shrinks, every crash point recovers, and a damaged snapshot fails loudly.
hints: Rename within a directory is atomic on POSIX. To make the rename itself durable, open the directory and `Sync` it.
Replaying the old log on top of a newer snapshot is safe because sets and deletes are idempotent in order.
Prefix the snapshot with a CRC32 of its contents, and refuse to open if it doesn't match.

levels.title: Overclock
levels.brief: Measure, profile, then batch fsyncs so writes stop queueing behind each other.
build: `WithSyncFunc` option and `Syncs()` counter
A writer goroutine that batches waiting appends
Sticky sync failures and a clean Close
levels.win: Concurrent appends share syncs (≤500 syncs for 2000 appends), each append still waits for its own sync, and failures poison the log.
hints: Each Append sends `request{rec, done chan error}` to the writer and waits on `done`.
Writer loop: block for one request, then drain more without blocking (`select` with `default`), write them all, sync once, reply to all.
Once a sync fails, remember the error and return it for every later batch without writing.

chapters.name: HTTP by Hand
chapters.line: Write an HTTP/1.1 server yourself on raw TCP. No net/http outside tests.

levels.title: Request Line
levels.brief: Speak HTTP over a raw socket and see exactly what a browser or curl sends you.
build: `ReadRequest(br)`, `Request`, `Header`
Error sentinels for 400 / 505 / 431
A Server answering everything with the hello page
levels.win: Parses everything valid, rejects 16 kinds of malformed request, enforces size limits, and serves net/http's client.
hints: Count bytes as you read lines and stop at 8 KiB. `br.ReadSlice('\n')` returns `bufio.ErrBufferFull` for long lines: keep appending.
`strings.Split(line, " ")` must give exactly three non-empty parts; a double space gives an empty one.
Header names are tokens: letters, digits and ``!#$%&'*+-.^_`|~``. A space before the colon makes the name invalid.

levels.title: Status and Body
levels.brief: Read request bodies and write proper responses.
build: `Handler`, `HandlerFunc`, `ResponseWriter`
Request bodies by Content-Length with limits
Correct heads for 204, 304 and HEAD; panic recovery
levels.win: net/http parses every response you write, bad lengths are 400, oversized 413, truncated bodies error, and no header injection gets through.
hints: Buffer the body in a `bytes.Buffer` and write the head after the handler returns, when you know the length.
Snapshot the headers when WriteHeader is called; later changes don't count.
`io.LimitReader` reports EOF when the underlying reader does. Write your own body reader that turns an early EOF into `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF`.

levels.title: Switchboard
levels.brief: Your own router, so handlers stop being one giant switch.
build: `Router` with method + path patterns and wildcards
404, 405 with Allow, specificity ranking
`KVRoutes` on a Store
levels.win: Routing, percent-decoding, specificity and the KV API all behave like Go 1.22's ServeMux.
hints: Parse patterns once at registration into segments: literal, `{name}`, or `{name...}`.
Score a match per segment (literal 2, wildcard 1, rest 0) and compare scores with `slices.Compare`.
Collect methods of routes whose path matched but method didn't: that's your Allow header.

levels.title: Keep-Alive
levels.brief: Serve many requests over one connection, and close idle ones.
build: A request loop per connection
Idle, header and per-connection limits
Drain unread bodies
levels.win: Pipelining, Connection rules, drained bodies, and all three timeouts behave like a production server.
hints: Use `br.Peek(1)` under the idle deadline to wait for the next request, then switch to the header deadline.
Drain with `io.Copy(io.Discard, io.LimitReader(body, 256<<10))`; if it hit the limit, close.
Decide `closeAfter` before calling the handler, so the response head can say `Connection: close`.

levels.title: Streaming
levels.brief: Send a response before you know how long it is.
build: `Flush()` and automatic chunked responses
A chunked request-body reader
`GET /v1/keys` streaming
levels.win: Data streams before the handler returns, chunked uploads decode, and every malformed case is rejected.
hints: Once the head is sent with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, each Write becomes `%x\r\n` + bytes + `\r\n`.
A chunked reader is a small state machine: read size line, read that many bytes, expect CRLF, repeat until size 0, then skip trailers to a blank line.
Reject sizes with more than 15 hex digits before parsing to avoid overflow.

levels.title: Conformance
levels.brief: Prove your server speaks real HTTP, then read how net/http does it.
build: `Server.Shutdown(ctx)`
`Expect: 100-continue`
Pass differential tests and fuzzing
levels.win: Your parser agrees with net/http, survives fuzzing, handles 1000 keep-alive requests, and shuts down gracefully.
hints: Reuse the idle/busy tracking from wire.Server. A connection waiting for its next request is idle.
Keep Request.Path escaped; net/http compares with `URL.EscapedPath()`.
When a fuzz test fails, Go saves the input under testdata/fuzz. Re-run `go test` to replay it.

chapters.name: net/http
chapters.line: Swap your hand-built server for net/http and see what it gives you.

levels.title: Front Panel
levels.brief: Rebuild the Chapter 4 API on net/http and compare how much code disappears.
build: `http.ServeMux` routes: `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE /v1/kv/{key}`
Read the key with `r.PathValue("key")`
JSON errors shaped `{"error": "..."}`
Keep your httpraw server around so you can compare the two
levels.win: The same curl commands from 4.3 work. A wrong method gets 405 with an `Allow` header, and a 2 MB body gets 413.
hints: `mux.HandleFunc("GET /v1/kv/{key}", h.get)`. Method patterns need Go 1.22 or later.
Write one `writeJSON(w, status, v)` helper and use it everywhere.
Set headers before `WriteHeader`. After the first `Write` they're locked, just like in your 4.2 writer.

levels.title: Signal Chain
levels.brief: Logging, request IDs and panic recovery as composable layers.
build: `type Middleware func(http.Handler) http.Handler` and a `chain()` helper
Request IDs from `crypto/rand`
A slog access log with status and duration
Recover from panics with a 500
levels.win: Every request logs one JSON line with id, method, path, status and duration. A handler that panics returns 500 and the server keeps serving.
hints: To capture the status, embed `http.ResponseWriter` in your own struct and override `WriteHeader`.
Use an unexported type for context keys: `type ctxKey struct{}`.
Put recovery outermost so it also catches panics in your other middleware.

levels.title: Watchdog
levels.brief: Make slow clients and slow disks unable to hang your server.
build: `http.Server` with `ReadHeaderTimeout`, `ReadTimeout`, `WriteTimeout`, `IdleTimeout`
A per-request deadline in middleware
Store methods return when `ctx` is done
`server.Shutdown(ctx)` wired to your signal handling from 2.5
levels.win: A store with an injected 5 second delay makes requests fail with 503 after your 1 second budget, and the store sees its context cancelled. Ctrl-C drains HTTP and TCP together.
hints: A zero-value `http.Server` has no timeouts. A slow client can hold a connection open forever.
`select { case <-ctx.Done(): return ctx.Err(); case res := <-work: ... }`
Map `context.DeadlineExceeded` to a status code in exactly one place.

levels.title: Test Jig
levels.brief: Test handlers end to end without starting servers by hand.
build: Unit tests per handler with `httptest.NewRecorder`
An integration test through the full middleware chain with `httptest.NewServer`
A fake Store for error paths
levels.win: `go test -race ./api/...` covers every route and status code from 5.1 plus the panic and timeout paths, in under 2 seconds.
hints: `NewServer` gives you a real URL, and `srv.Client()` is preconfigured for it.
Fake the Store interface for error paths instead of corrupting real files.
`t.Cleanup(srv.Close)` keeps tests tidy.

levels.title: Gauges
levels.brief: See inside the running server.
build: `/healthz` and `/readyz`
expvar counters: requests, errors, keys, open connections
`net/http/pprof` on a separate admin port
A log level you can change at runtime
levels.win: `curl :7071/debug/vars` shows your counters climbing under load, and `go tool pprof http://localhost:7071/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=10` opens a profile.
hints: Importing `net/http/pprof` registers on `http.DefaultServeMux`. Serve that mux only on the admin port.
`slog.LevelVar` can change while the server runs.
Readiness should fail while the store is still loading (WAL replay, once you have one). Liveness shouldn't.

chapters.name: Watch
chapters.line: Optional. Live change feeds: pub/sub with channels and server-sent events.

levels.title: Fan-out
levels.brief: An in-process broker that tells subscribers when keys change, without letting slow readers stall writes.
build: The store publishes an event on every Set and Delete
`Subscribe(prefix) (<-chan Event, func())` returns a channel and an unsubscribe function
Buffered subscriber channels; a subscriber that falls too far behind gets disconnected
levels.win: With one subscriber that never reads, 1,000 writes take no longer than with none, and that subscriber is dropped. Fast subscribers see every event in order.
hints: `select { case ch <- ev: default: /* this subscriber is too slow */ }`
Make unsubscribe safe to call twice with `sync.Once`.
Only the broker closes subscriber channels. Sending on a closed channel panics.

levels.title: Event Stream
levels.brief: Push changes to HTTP clients as server-sent events.
build: `GET /v1/watch?prefix=user:` streams events as `text/event-stream`
A heartbeat comment every 15 seconds
Unsubscribe when the client disconnects
levels.win: `curl -N 'localhost:8080/v1/watch?prefix=user:'` prints an event within a second of `PUT /v1/kv/user:1`. Closing curl drops the subscriber count back down.
hints: `rc := http.NewResponseController(w)` then `rc.Flush()` after each event.
SSE is plain text: `data: ...` followed by a blank line. A line starting with `:` is a comment, handy as a heartbeat.
`<-r.Context().Done()` fires when the client goes away.

levels.title: Resume
levels.brief: Clients that reconnect pick up exactly where they left off.
build: Monotonic event IDs sent as `id:` lines
A ring buffer of recent events
Honour the `Last-Event-ID` header on reconnect
levels.win: Kill curl, write 5 keys, reconnect with `-H 'Last-Event-ID: <last id>'`: the 5 missed events arrive first, then live ones, with no gaps or duplicates.
hints: Subscribe first, then replay from the buffer, then skip live events you've already replayed.
A fixed-size slice plus a head index is a ring buffer. No extra package needed.
If the requested ID is older than the buffer, send a special event saying so rather than silently skipping.

chapters.name: Traffic Control
chapters.line: Optional. Rate limiting, caching and request coalescing for real web traffic.

levels.title: Token Bucket
levels.brief: Rate-limit clients by IP with a token bucket middleware.
build: A token bucket per client IP: refill rate and burst size
`429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header
Stale buckets cleaned up in the background
levels.win: Twenty quick curls show 200s then 429s with `Retry-After`. A test with an injected clock proves tokens refill at the right rate.
hints: Refill lazily: on each request add `elapsed × rate` tokens, capped at the burst size.
`net.SplitHostPort(r.RemoteAddr)` gives you the client IP.
Unused buckets leak memory. Sweep them with the janitor pattern from 1.4.

levels.title: LRU Cache
levels.brief: A read-through cache in front of a slow store.
build: An LRU cache bounded by total bytes, built on `container/list` and a map
Invalidate on Set and Delete
Hit and miss counters in expvar
levels.win: Tests prove eviction order. With a store that takes 50 ms per read, cache hits return in under a millisecond, and the counters show the hit rate.
hints: Map each key to its `*list.Element` and move it to the front on every hit.
Forget invalidation and the cache serves stale data. Test that case first.
Try writing it as `LRU[K comparable, V any]`. It's a good first generics exercise.

levels.title: Single Flight
levels.brief: Collapse a stampede of identical cache misses into one store read.
build: Concurrent misses for the same key share one in-flight call
Every waiter gets the same value or the same error
The in-flight entry is removed when the call finishes
levels.win: 100 concurrent GETs for one cold key cause exactly 1 store read, and all 100 get the value. A failed read is shared too, but isn't cached.
hints: Keep a `map[string]*call` where `call` holds a `WaitGroup`, the value and the error.
The first caller does the work. Everyone else calls `Wait()` and reads the result.
Delete the map entry when the call finishes, so the next miss tries again.

chapters.name: Queues
chapters.line: Optional. Azure Service Bus fundamentals, built yourself: peek-lock, dead letters, scheduling and duplicate detection.

levels.title: Mailbox
levels.brief: A durable queue broker speaking your frame protocol, carrying the same message shape Service Bus uses.
build: A `Message` with `MessageID`, `Body`, `ContentType`, `CorrelationID`, `Subject` and `ApplicationProperties`, plus broker-set `SequenceNumber` and `EnqueuedTime`
Named queues; `Send` and `Receive` in receive-and-delete mode
Every send goes through your Chapter 3 WAL before it's acknowledged
`burrowctl bus send orders <body>` and `burrowctl bus receive orders`
levels.win: Send 1,000 messages, `kill -9` the broker, restart: you receive all 1,000 exactly once, in order, with sequence numbers that only go up.
hints: Service Bus has two receive modes. Receive-and-delete is at-most-once: if your consumer crashes after receiving, the message is gone. The next level fixes that.
The broker assigns sequence numbers, never the client. Rebuild the counter from the WAL on replay.
Keep bodies as `[]byte`. Real Service Bus bodies are opaque bytes too; the content type tells consumers how to read them.

levels.title: Peek-Lock
levels.brief: Receive without losing messages: lock a message while you work on it, then settle it.
build: Peek-lock `Receive` returns the message plus a random `LockToken` and `LockedUntil`
`Complete`, `Abandon` and `RenewLock` by lock token
Locks expire after the queue's `LockDuration` (Service Bus defaults to 1 minute, max 5) and the message becomes available again
`DeliveryCount` goes up when a message is abandoned or its lock expires
levels.win: Receive and walk away: once the lock expires the message comes back with `DeliveryCount` 2. Completing with an expired token fails with `ErrLockLost`. All proven with an injected clock.
hints: A message is available, locked or gone. Draw the transitions before you code them.
One goroutine watching a min-heap ordered by `LockedUntil` scales better than a `time.AfterFunc` per message. Try both and compare.
At-least-once means consumers will see duplicates. Peek-lock trades lost messages for repeated ones.

levels.title: Dead Letters
levels.brief: Poison and expired messages go somewhere you can inspect, instead of looping forever.
build: Each queue gets a sub-queue at `orders/$deadletterqueue`
Past `MaxDeliveryCount` (default 10) a message moves there with reason `MaxDeliveryCountExceeded`
Consumers can call `DeadLetter(token, reason, description)` themselves
Per-message `TimeToLive`: expired messages are dropped, or dead-lettered with `TTLExpiredException` when the queue opts in
`burrowctl bus resubmit orders` moves dead letters back
levels.win: A consumer that always abandons puts its message in the DLQ after 10 deliveries, with the right reason. An expired message lands there only on queues with dead-lettering on expiry turned on.
hints: A dead-letter queue is just another queue with a special name. Reuse everything.
Check expiry when handing a message out, not only in the sweeper. Never deliver an expired message.
The DLQ is where on-call starts. Keep `DeadLetterReason`, `DeadLetterErrorDescription` and the delivery count on the message.

levels.title: Scheduled and Deferred
levels.brief: Messages that arrive in the future, and messages a consumer sets aside to handle later.
build: `ScheduleMessage(msg, enqueueAt)` returns a sequence number; `CancelScheduled(seq)` removes it
A min-heap releases scheduled messages on time
`Defer(token)` hides a locked message from normal receives
`ReceiveDeferred(seqs...)` is the only way to get deferred messages back
levels.win: A message scheduled 5 minutes out is invisible until the injected clock passes it, then arrives normally. A deferred message never comes back from `Receive`, only from `ReceiveDeferred` with its sequence number.
hints: `container/heap` needs Len, Less, Swap, Push and Pop on your type. Less compares enqueue times.
Sleep until the earliest scheduled time, but wake early when something sooner is scheduled. `select` on a timer and a wake channel does it.
Deferral is for out-of-order workflows: step 3 arrived before step 2, so park step 3 and remember its sequence number.

levels.title: Duplicate Detection
levels.brief: Senders retry after timeouts. The broker drops the copies.
build: Queues opt in with `RequiresDuplicateDetection` and a time window
A repeated `MessageID` inside the window is acknowledged but silently discarded
IDs fall out of the window as time passes
The set of recent IDs survives restarts
levels.win: A test sends, fakes a timeout and resends with the same `MessageID`: the consumer sees one message. Once the window passes, the same ID is accepted again.
hints: A map for lookup plus a list ordered by arrival for expiry. Same shape as an LRU cache.
The sender must reuse the same `MessageID` on retry. Generating a fresh ID per attempt defeats the feature.
This only dedupes sends. Consumers still need to be idempotent, because peek-lock redelivers.

levels.title: Competing Consumers
levels.brief: Many workers drain one queue quickly without processing anything twice.
build: Long-polling `Receive(ctx, max)` that waits for messages instead of busy-looping
Client-side prefetch of up to N locked messages
Several consumers competing on one queue
Locks on prefetched messages keep ticking while they sit in the buffer
levels.win: Three consumers drain 10,000 messages: every message is completed once and each consumer handles at least 25%. With a large prefetch and slow consumers, a test shows buffered locks expiring and those messages being redelivered.
hints: A blocked receiver should wake when a message arrives. `sync.Cond` or a notify channel per queue both work.
Prefetch trades latency for lock time. The lock starts when the broker hands the message over, not when your code reads it.
Service Bus clients do this over AMQP with link credit: the receiver tells the broker how many messages it can take.

chapters.name: Topics & Sessions
chapters.line: Optional. Pub/sub with filtered subscriptions, ordered sessions, transactions, then the real Azure Service Bus.

levels.title: Fan-out Topics
levels.brief: One send, many independent copies: topics with subscriptions.
build: `CreateTopic(name)` and `CreateSubscription(topic, name)`
A send to a topic copies the message into every subscription
Each subscription is a full queue: peek-lock, delivery count, DLQ
Paths like `events/Subscriptions/billing` and `events/Subscriptions/billing/$deadletterqueue`
levels.win: Three subscriptions each get their own copy. Completing in `billing` doesn't touch `audit`. A subscription nobody reads keeps filling, and its DLQ works independently.
hints: Subscriptions are your Queues-chapter queue with a different name. If you're writing new settlement code, something is off.
Copy the message per subscription so a property set in one can't leak into another.
Write the whole fan-out as one WAL record, so a crash can't deliver to some subscriptions and not others.

levels.title: Filters
levels.brief: Subscriptions choose which messages they want, using rules you parse and evaluate yourself.
build: Correlation filters matching `CorrelationID`, `Subject` and application properties
A lexer and recursive-descent parser for a SQL filter subset, like `region = 'au' AND (amount > 100 OR priority IN ('high', 'urgent'))`
Evaluate the parsed tree against each message
A default rule that matches everything; a subscription whose rules don't match gets nothing
levels.win: Table tests cover precedence (`AND` before `OR`), parentheses, strings, numbers, `IN`, `IS NULL` and `NOT`. Messages route only to subscriptions whose rules match. A malformed rule is rejected when it's created, not when a message arrives.
hints: Lexer first: turn the string into tokens (identifier, string, number, operator, keyword) and test it on its own.
One parse function per precedence level: `parseOr` calls `parseAnd`, which calls `parseNot`, which calls `parseComparison`.
Give each node an `Eval(msg) (any, error)` method. Comparing an `int` with a `float64` decoded from JSON is where the bugs hide.

levels.title: Sessions
levels.brief: Strict ordering per customer, while different customers are processed in parallel.
build: Messages carry a `SessionID`; session-enabled entities reject messages without one
`AcceptNextSession` locks a whole session to one receiver
Messages within a session come out strictly in order
`GetSessionState` and `SetSessionState` store a small blob per session
levels.win: Three interleaved sessions and two receivers: each session is handled by one receiver at a time, in order, and session state survives a broker restart.
hints: A session lock is a peek-lock on a whole session instead of one message. Reuse your expiry machinery.
Session state is how a consumer remembers where it is in a workflow, like a tiny per-key database.
This is Service Bus's answer to ordering and parallelism at once. It's close to one OTP process per key.

levels.title: Forwarding and Transactions
levels.brief: Chain entities together, and settle one message while sending others, all or nothing.
build: Auto-forward: a queue or subscription with `ForwardTo` pushes everything into another entity
A hop counter that dead-letters with `MaxTransferHopCountExceeded` when forwarding loops
A transaction that completes an input message and sends output messages atomically
Each transaction commits as a single WAL record
levels.win: A forwarding loop between two queues dead-letters instead of spinning forever. Killing the broker mid-transaction never leaves the input completed without its outputs, or outputs sent while the input is still pending.
hints: A transaction here is a list of operations applied together. Write them as one WAL record and the crash test passes for free.
Keep the hop count in a broker-owned property. Never trust a counter the client can set.
It's the transactional outbox pattern, moved into the broker.

levels.title: The Real Thing
levels.brief: Point the same scenarios at Azure Service Bus and see how close you got.
build: Run the Azure Service Bus emulator in Docker, with queues, topics and subscriptions declared in its `config.json`
A separate module, `azcompare/`, using the official `azservicebus` Go SDK. This is the only place in the curriculum you add a dependency
Port your peek-lock, dead-letter, filter and session tests so they run against both Burrow and the emulator
Write a short table of what matched and what didn't
levels.win: The same scenario suite passes against Burrow and the emulator, or fails in ways your table explains.
hints: The emulator doesn't keep data across container restarts, so your `kill -9` tests only make sense against Burrow.
Map names as you go: `CompleteMessage`, `AbandonMessage`, `DeadLetterMessage`, `DeferMessage`, `RenewMessageLock`, `AcceptNextSessionForQueue`.
Real Service Bus speaks AMQP 1.0 over TCP. Your frame protocol plays the same role. Read the AMQP spec's settlement section with fresh eyes.

chapters.name: Cluster
chapters.line: Many nodes: RPC, membership, sharding and quorums.

levels.title: Multi-core
levels.brief: Run three Burrow nodes on one machine from a single command.
build: Node flags: `-id`, `-http`, `-peer-addr`, `-data`
`cmd/devcluster` starts three burrowd processes with `os/exec`
Prefix each node's log lines (`n1 |`, `n2 |`)
Ctrl-C stops them all
levels.win: `go run ./cmd/devcluster` starts n1 to n3 with prefixed logs. After Ctrl-C, `pgrep burrowd` finds nothing.
hints: `cmd.StdoutPipe()` plus a `bufio.Scanner` gives you lines to prefix.
`exec.CommandContext` kills children when the context ends.
Give each node its own `-data` directory now, so their WALs won't collide once you add persistence.

levels.title: Interconnect
levels.brief: Nodes talk to each other over your own frame codec.
build: RPC on top of the 2.3 frames: request IDs and a method byte
Many calls multiplexed over one connection
A reader goroutine routes replies by ID
Timeouts from `ctx`
levels.win: 1,000 concurrent calls from n1 to n2 over one TCP connection all return correctly. Killing n2 mid-flight fails every pending call promptly instead of hanging.
hints: Keep pending calls in a `map[uint64]chan reply` guarded by a mutex. Writers lock only around the write.
When the reader goroutine exits, walk the pending map and fail every call.
This is roughly how `net/rpc` works. Read its `client.go` after you finish.

levels.title: Heartbeat
levels.brief: Every node knows which nodes are alive.
build: A membership list with per-peer state: alive, suspect, dead
Periodic pings over your RPC
Suspect after missed pings, dead after a timeout
`GET /v1/cluster` shows the view
levels.win: Kill n3: within 5 seconds n1 and n2 mark it suspect, then dead. Restart it and it returns to alive. Every node shows the same view.
hints: Add jitter so nodes don't all ping on the same tick.
Give the state type a `String()` method and your logs read themselves.
You can't tell a dead node from a slow one. Write down what your timeouts trade off.

levels.title: Address Decoder
levels.brief: Spread keys across nodes so each one owns a slice of the keyspace.
build: A hash ring with virtual nodes using `hash/fnv`
Lookups with a sorted slice and `slices.BinarySearch`
Any node forwards a request to the key's owner
levels.win: 10,000 keys land within ±15% of even across 3 nodes. Removing a node moves only about a third of the keys. A GET to any node returns the right value.
hints: Hash each node 100 or more times (`n1#0`, `n1#1`, ...) for an even spread.
Find the first ring point at or after `hash(key)`, wrapping to the start.
Add a header like `X-Burrow-Forwarded` to stop requests bouncing between nodes.

levels.title: Redundancy
levels.brief: Store each key on three nodes and survive losing one.
build: N=3 replicas chosen from the ring
Writes fan out in parallel and succeed at W=2 acks
Reads ask R=2 and return the newest version
Cancel the slow replica once quorum is met; repair stale copies on read
levels.win: With one node down, reads and writes still succeed. After it restarts, read repair brings its copy up to date. Goroutine counts match before and after a test.
hints: Buffer the results channel to N so late replies never block.
Return as soon as you have W successes, or as soon as W becomes impossible.
Last-write-wins with timestamps is simple and wrong under clock skew. Note why; Chapter 7 fixes it.

chapters.name: Consensus
chapters.line: Raft, from leader election to a replicated KV store.

levels.title: Election
levels.brief: Nodes agree on one leader per term.
build: Follower, candidate and leader roles
Randomised election timeouts and the RequestVote RPC
One goroutine owns all Raft state and handles events in a `select` loop
levels.win: Three nodes elect exactly one leader within 2 seconds. Kill it and a new leader with a higher term appears within 3 seconds. A test harness asserts there are never two leaders in one term.
hints: Read Figure 2 of the Raft paper and keep it open. It is the spec.
One goroutine owning the state replaces most locks. It will feel familiar from OTP processes.
Run the harness with `-count=100`. Election bugs only appear sometimes.

levels.title: Log Shipping
levels.brief: The leader replicates a log; entries commit once a majority has them.
build: AppendEntries with the `prevLogIndex` and `prevLogTerm` check
`nextIndex` and `matchIndex` per follower
Advance `commitIndex`; heartbeats are empty AppendEntries
levels.win: Partition a follower, write 100 entries, heal it: it catches up and all three logs are identical.
hints: On rejection, decrement `nextIndex` and retry. Optimise later.
Only count replicas to commit entries from the current term (Figure 8 in the paper).
Log every RPC with its term and indexes while debugging. You will need it.

levels.title: State Machine
levels.brief: Put the KV store on top of Raft for linearizable writes.
build: Apply committed entries to your Store in order
Client writes go to the leader and wait for commit and apply
Followers redirect with 307 to the leader
Reads go through the leader with a read-index check
levels.win: Writes through any node reach the leader and survive a leader failover. Followers never serve stale reads in the default mode.
hints: Keep a `map[index]chan result` so the HTTP handler can wait for its own entry.
If the term changes before your entry commits, return a leadership error.
Read-index: note `commitIndex`, confirm leadership with one heartbeat round, wait until applied reaches it.

levels.title: Non-volatile
levels.brief: Make Raft survive full restarts by reusing your WAL.
build: Persist `currentTerm`, `votedFor` and log entries with the Chapter 3 WAL before replying to RPCs
Snapshots via your 3.3 compaction
InstallSnapshot for followers that fall far behind
levels.win: Restart all three nodes at once: no acknowledged write is lost and terms never go backwards.
go: what must be durable, and when
hints: Persist before you respond. Voting twice in one term after a crash breaks safety.
Your CRC guard from 3.2 now protects consensus state.
InstallSnapshot can wait until everything else works.

chapters.name: Chaos
chapters.line: Break it on purpose and prove it holds.

levels.title: Fault Injector
levels.brief: A network proxy that makes the cluster's life miserable.
build: A TCP proxy between nodes that can delay, drop and partition connections
A small HTTP admin API to control it
devcluster routes node-to-node traffic through it
levels.win: `curl -X POST ':9000/partition?nodes=n1'` isolates n1, the other two elect a leader, and healing reunites the cluster.
hints: Use two goroutines per proxied connection, one per direction.
Seed the random source so a failing run can be replayed exactly.
Delaying each chunk with `time.Sleep` is fine here. This is test tooling.

levels.title: History Checker
levels.brief: Record what clients saw and prove the cluster didn't lie.
build: A load generator that logs each operation with start time, end time and result
A checker: every acknowledged write is readable later, and reads of a key never go back in time
levels.win: A clean run passes. Deliberately serving reads from followers makes the checker fail and name the bad operation.
hints: Write histories as JSON lines so you can inspect failures with jq.
Start with "no lost acknowledged writes". It catches most bugs.
Full linearizability checking is hard. Porcupine and Jepsen's Knossos are the references if you want to go further.

levels.title: Leader Down
levels.brief: Final boss. Kill the leader during a write storm. Burrow must keep its promises.
build: A scenario runner: start devcluster behind the chaos proxy
Run the load generator, `kill -9` the leader, partition a follower
Heal, restart, then run the checker
levels.win: 10 consecutive seeded runs pass the checker with zero lost acknowledged writes, using only the Go standard library.
hints: When it fails, replay the seed and read the RPC logs you added in 7.2.
Expect to find bugs in chapters you thought were finished. That's the game working.
When it passes, write the README. You've built a distributed database.
